entries.question: Do angels have sex?
entries.summary: Genesis 6:2-4 and Jude 6-7 describe angelic beings (the 'sons of God') having sex with human women and producing Nephilim. Genesis 19 has the Sodomites attempting to rape two angelic visitors. Mark 12:25 then has Jesus saying angels in heaven neither marry nor are given in marriage. The Bible's angelic sexuality is inconsistent — actively horny in Genesis and Jude, genderless in the Synoptics.
entries.commentary: Apologists try to split this two ways. First, they reinterpret Genesis 6:2 so the 'sons of God' are not angels at all but the godly Sethite line, with 'daughters of men' as wicked Cainite women. Archer and Hamilton both run this move. Second, they note Jesus says angels don't marry 'in heaven' — which leaves open the possibility of fallen angels acting otherwise. The Sethite reading is a post-biblical rationalization. Michael Heiser in The Unseen Realm, Loren Stuckenbruck's work on 1 Enoch, and James VanderKam all document that Second Temple Judaism unanimously read Genesis 6:2 as referring to angelic beings — it's the standard reading in 1 Enoch 6-11, Jubilees 5, the Damascus Document, Josephus, Philo, and the New Testament authors including Jude and 2 Peter. Jude 6-7 explicitly glosses Genesis 6 as angels 'going after strange flesh' (sarkos heteras). The Sethite interpretation only emerges in the third and fourth centuries CE with Julius Africanus and Augustine, largely motivated by theological embarrassment at the earlier reading. So the contradiction is real: early biblical writers held that a category of divine beings sexually interacted with humans, and the Synoptic Jesus treats angels as categorically asexual. The harmonization requires throwing out the Second Temple consensus reading of Genesis 6.

answers.answer: No, angels neither marry nor have sex (not in heaven, anyway).
answers.answer_explanation:
For when they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given
				    in marriage; but are as the angels which are in heaven. Mark 12:25

commentary_out.commentary:
The entry juxtaposes three data points. Genesis 6:1-4 and Jude 6-7 describe divine beings ('sons of God,' angels) producing offspring with human women; Genesis 19 has the men of Sodom seeking to 'know' (Hebrew yada) two angelic visitors; and Mark 12:25 has Jesus declare that the resurrected 'neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels in heaven.' The question at issue is whether angelic beings are sexual creatures, and the texts pull in opposite directions.

Apologists pursue two non-angelic harmonizations of Genesis 6, and a steel-man must engage the strongest forms of each. The weaker is the Sethite reading: the bene ha-elohim of Genesis 6:2 are the godly line of Seth and the 'daughters of men' are wicked Cainite women, making 6:1-4 a story of compromised intermarriage between covenant and pagan lines. Gleason Archer and, with qualifications, Victor Hamilton entertain versions of this. A stronger contemporary alternative is the dynastic or divine-king interpretation, defended in detail by Meredith Kline ('Divine Kingship and Genesis 6:1-4,' WTJ 24 [1962]: 187-204), which takes bene ha-elohim as royal figures — ancient Near Eastern kings styled 'sons of the god' — exercising the despotic polygamy and droit du seigneur the narrative implicitly condemns. This reading draws genuine support from the immediate context: Genesis 6:3, wedged between the union and the Nephilim notice, restricts the lifespan of man ('his days shall be an hundred and twenty years'), focusing the divine response on human flesh and human transgression rather than on a celestial revolt. On this view the offspring are gibborim, 'mighty men,' heroic human despots, not hybrids. The second harmonization concerns the scope of Mark 12:25: Jesus speaks of angels 'in heaven,' arguably leaving open that fallen angels who 'kept not their first estate' (Jude 6) might behave otherwise.

These are the strongest forms of the case, and the contextual argument from 6:3 has real purchase. Yet the angelic reading better fits both the phrase and, decisively, its reception. Bene ha-elohim elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible denotes divine-council members (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; the cognate bene elim in Ps 29:1; 89:6), never a human lineage as such; Michael Heiser's treatment of the divine council marshals this lexical evidence. More telling is the unanimous early reception. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6-16) develops the episode at length — angels under Shemihazah and Asael descend, take wives, and beget the giant Nephilim — and Jubilees 5, the Damascus Document (CD 2:17-19), Josephus (Antiquities 1.73, where the 'angels of God' beget sons), and Philo all assume the angelic reading. Loren Stuckenbruck's The Myth of Rebellious Angels and James VanderKam's Enoch document this as the dominant Second Temple interpretation; Archie Wright's The Origin of Evil Spirits traces the reception in granular detail. The New Testament authors stand squarely inside that tradition: Jude 6-7 brackets the angels 'who kept not their first estate' with Sodom and Gomorrah, which 'in like manner' gave themselves to fornication and went after 'strange flesh' (Greek sarkos heteras, 'other/different flesh') — language presupposing the angel-human crossing — and Jude 14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 directly as prophecy; 2 Peter 2:4 echoes the same tradition, casting the offending angels into tartaros. Richard Bauckham's commentary on Jude makes the dependence explicit. The Sethite reading proper surfaces only in the third and fourth centuries (Julius Africanus floats it; Augustine, City of God 15.23, promotes it), largely from theological discomfort with copulating angels once a more transcendent angelology had taken hold.

That history undercuts the harmonization for the texts that matter most. The biblical writers behind Genesis 6 and behind Jude/2 Peter held that a class of divine beings interacted sexually with humans. Genesis 19 is a weaker leg of the contradiction: the visitors are malakim (messengers/angels), but the Sodomites' intent presumably targets beings they take for human men, so the episode speaks more to human predation than to angelic sexuality per se. Genesis 6 and Jude carry the weight. Against them, the Synoptic Jesus deploys angelic asexuality as the very premise that defeats the Sadducees' levirate puzzle (Mark 12:25); the 'in heaven' qualifier does not rescue the harmonization, because the rhetorical force of the argument requires that angels by kind do not reproduce. The dynastic reading, even at its strongest, must overturn the Second Temple consensus that the biblical authors themselves shared.

Verdict: genuine contradiction — the angelic sexuality of Genesis 6 and Jude reflects the Watchers tradition the biblical writers held, against which the Synoptic Jesus treats angels as categorically asexual; both the Sethite and the stronger dynastic harmonizations require setting aside the reading the New Testament authors themselves endorsed.

entries.question: Who was the father of Salah?
entries.summary: Genesis 10:24 and 11:12 both have Arphaxad directly fathering Salah. Luke 3:35-36 inserts a generation — 'Salah, which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad' — making Cainan an intermediate ancestor.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest textual-critical contradictions in the whole enterprise. Apologists like Archer and Glenn Morton argue Luke is following the Greek Septuagint, which does include a second Cainan at Gen 10:24 (LXX), and thus Luke's genealogy reflects a legitimate variant textual tradition. That's empirically true — the LXX of Gen 10:24 and 11:12-13 does insert Cainan. The problem is that the name appears to be a scribal expansion in the LXX tradition that has no support in the Masoretic Hebrew, the Samaritan Pentateuch, or the Qumran Genesis fragments. Emanuel Tov's textual-critical work treats the LXX Cainan as a secondary addition designed to harmonize generational counts. So the apologist either has to say (a) Luke faithfully recorded a corrupt Greek text, which means scripture transmits a genealogical error with divine authority, or (b) the MT is itself defective and the LXX preserved the original — which almost no critical textual scholar endorses and which would require rewriting every Hebrew genealogy. Either way, Luke 3:36 is in direct conflict with the Hebrew text of Genesis on a basic paternity question. The LXX defense doesn't eliminate the contradiction, it just moves which Bible contains it.

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 10:24 and 11:12 in the Masoretic Hebrew make Arphaxad the direct father of Salah (Shelah): 'Arphaxad begat Salah.' Luke 3:35-36, tracing Jesus' ancestry backward, inserts a generation: 'Sala, which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad.' Luke thus places a second Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah whom the Hebrew genealogy does not know. (A first Cainan/Kenan appears legitimately in the antediluvian line at Gen 5:9, son of Enosh; the dispute concerns the second, postdiluvian Cainan.)

The apologetic case, advanced by Gleason Archer and others, is that Luke faithfully followed the Septuagint, and the LXX of Genesis does in fact contain this second Cainan. This is empirically correct and important: the major LXX manuscripts read a Kainan between Arphaxad and Sala at Genesis 10:24 and again in the chronological genealogy of 11:12-13, assigning him a 130-year span. Luke was therefore not inventing the name; he reproduced a Greek Vorlage that already carried it. The harmonization that 'Luke and the LXX simply preserve a generation the MT dropped' is a real textual possibility, not special pleading, and deserves to be stated at full strength.

The weight of the text-critical evidence, however, runs against the originality of the second Cainan. It is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew and absent from the Samaritan Pentateuch, as well as from Josephus's genealogical reckoning. The Qumran evidence is best stated cautiously: the relevant portions of Genesis 10-11 are poorly preserved among the Qumran Genesis fragments, so they furnish at most weak and indirect support rather than a clear positive witness against the second Cainan — the decisive Hebrew testimony is the MT-plus-Samaritan agreement. Within the LXX tradition itself the name is suspected of being a secondary intrusion, likely arising from the symmetrical structuring of the postdiluvian list (giving it ten generations to match the antediluvian ten), or from a copyist's eye duplicating an entry within the formulaic 'X lived N years and begat Y' pattern — a mechanism akin to dittography or homoeoteleuton in stereotyped lines. The same schematizing impulse is visible in the book of Jubilees, which reworks the postdiluvian generations to fit its own chronological frame, and reflects the broader tendency of LXX Genesis chronology toward systematized, schematic figures. Emanuel Tov classes the LXX postdiluvian chronology among its systematic harmonizing and schematizing expansions; Ronald Hendel's critical edition of Genesis 1-11 treats the second Cainan as a secondary plus in the Greek tradition.

A further textual wrinkle concerns Luke's own transmission. The earliest substantial witness to Luke 3, P75 (Papyrus Bodmer XIV-XV), does in fact contain the second Cainan, so the papyrus is regularly cited as evidence for Cainan being in Luke. The name is, however, omitted in Codex Bezae (D), whose genealogy is arranged differently. The scholarly question of whether Cainan was original to Luke therefore does not turn on P75; it turns on the argument that Luke 3:36 may have been conformed to the LXX in the course of transmission, an option discussed in I. Howard Marshall's NIGTC and elsewhere. Even if Cainan is original to Luke, that only strengthens the contradiction rather than dissolving it.

This leaves the apologist on the horns of a dilemma. Either (a) Luke accurately recorded the LXX, in which case an inspired New Testament genealogy transmits a name that the best Hebrew and Samaritan evidence shows was a secondary scribal addition — Scripture canonizing a textual error; or (b) the MT and Samaritan Pentateuch are both defective and the LXX uniquely preserved the original Cainan — a position virtually no text critic holds, since it would require positing independent loss of the same name across otherwise-divergent Hebrew traditions. Either way, Luke 3:36 stands in direct conflict with the Hebrew text of Genesis on a basic question of paternity. The LXX defense does not dissolve the contradiction; it relocates it, identifying which textual stream carries the discrepancy.

Verdict: a genuine contradiction rooted in a scribal expansion in the Septuagint tradition that Luke (or Luke's transmission) inherited; harmonizable only by abandoning the priority of the Hebrew text.

entries.question: Is incest forbidden?
entries.summary: Leviticus 18 and 20 and Deuteronomy 27 explicitly criminalize sex between half-siblings who share a father — it's called "a wicked thing" and draws a curse. Genesis 20:12 has Abraham calmly explain that Sarah is his half-sister on his father's side and also his wife, and God blesses the marriage in Genesis 17:16. Either the Torah's incest code applies to the patriarchs or it doesn't.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Walton run two different harmonizations here, and they don't combine well. The first move is chronological: the Levitical code hadn't been given yet in Abraham's time, so he wasn't under it. The second move is textual: maybe "sister" in Genesis 20:12 means something looser, like cousin or clanswoman, and Abraham was fudging to protect himself from Pharaoh. Pick one — they pull in opposite directions. The chronological defense concedes the contradiction in principle (Abraham would have been breaking the later law if it applied) and just pushes it behind a dispensational wall. The "loose sister" defense has to explain why Genesis 20:12 goes out of its way to specify "the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother" — that level of precision is the exact half-sister relationship Leviticus 18:9 explicitly forbids. Critical scholarship treats this as obvious: the patriarchal narratives preserve older legal and social norms (sister-wife marriage is attested in ancient Near Eastern royal houses), and the Levitical and Deuteronomic codes reflect later priestly and Deuteronomic systematization. The contradiction is real; the harmonization requires you to both admit and deny that Torah applies to the patriarchs in the same breath.
entries.scholarship: Jacob Milgrom, *Leviticus 17-22* (Anchor Bible 3A; Doubleday, 2000), on Lev 18:9. Nahum M. Sarna, *Genesis* (JPS Torah Commentary; Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Calum Carmichael, *Law, Legend, and Incest in the Bible: Leviticus 18-20* (Cornell University Press, 1997). Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982). John H. Walton, *Genesis* (NIV Application Commentary; Zondervan, 2001). Gordon J. Wenham, *Genesis 16-50* (Word Biblical Commentary 2; Word, 1994).

commentary_out.commentary:
The Holiness Code and the Deuteronomic curses are emphatic and specific. Leviticus 18:9 forbids uncovering the nakedness of 'thy sister, the daughter of thy father, or daughter of thy mother'; Leviticus 20:17 calls union with 'his father's daughter, or his mother's daughter' a 'wicked thing' (Hebrew chesed) and stipulates that the offenders 'shall be cut off' (wenikretu); Deuteronomy 27:22 lays a public curse on the man 'that lieth with his sister, the daughter of his father, or the daughter of his mother.' A philological note is warranted: the term rendered 'wicked thing' in Lev 20:17 is chesed in the sense of 'disgrace/shame,' and its relationship to the common covenant-loyalty word chesed ('steadfast love') is debated — many lexicographers treat the disgrace-term as a homonym from a separate root rather than the loyalty word used pejoratively, so the rhetorical irony sometimes drawn from it should be advanced cautiously. Genesis 20:12 has Abraham explain of Sarah, 'she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife,' and Genesis 17:16 has God bless that very marriage with the promise of Isaac. The relationship Abraham describes is, word for word, the paternal half-sister union that Leviticus 18:9 and Deuteronomy 27:22 single out for prohibition and curse.

Two distinct harmonizations are offered, and the central critical observation is that they pull in opposite directions and cannot be held together. The first is chronological and is the genuinely sound one: the Sinai legislation had not yet been given in Abraham's day, so the narrative does not portray him violating a law then in force. This is internally consistent — the Torah itself presents the incest code as Mosaic, post-dating the patriarchs by centuries — and it has a clear analogue in the standard treatment of Cain's wife and of Genesis's pre-Sinai world generally, where marriage among close kin is unavoidable and passes without comment. On the formal legal question, then, the contradiction does dissolve: Abraham is not depicted as a lawbreaker, only as a man living before the law. Archer and Walton both rely on this move.

The second harmonization is lexical: perhaps 'sister' (achot) in Genesis 20:12 is used loosely, in the broad Semitic sense that can cover a niece, cousin, or kinswoman, with Abraham shading the truth to protect himself in a foreign court. This defense fails on the text's own precision. Genesis 20:12 does not leave 'sister' vague; it specifies the exact degree — same father, different mother — which is precisely the half-sister relationship Leviticus isolates. The verse's specificity is the problem, not the solution. And the two defenses are mutually undermining: the lexical defense denies that any incest occurred, while the chronological defense concedes that it did but excuses it as pre-legal. One cannot consistently claim both that Sarah was not really Abraham's half-sister and that it would not have mattered if she were.

Critical scholarship reads the data as a straightforward layering of social and legal history. Nahum Sarna and Gordon Wenham note that close-kin marriages were socially acceptable in the patriarchal milieu, and the three sister-wife episodes (Gen 12, 20, 26) form a recognized narrative doublet preserving an older endogamous norm. A caution is needed on the comparative side: the once-influential thesis of Ephraim Speiser, who connected the sister-wife motif to a supposed Hurrian 'wife-sister adoption' custom at Nuzi, has been largely rejected by subsequent scholarship — Samuel Greengus showed the Nuzi texts do not attest the institution Speiser reconstructed — so it should not be leaned on as live support for the patriarchal practice. The narratives themselves, not a discredited Nuzi parallel, are the evidence that such unions were once tellable without scandal. Jacob Milgrom's analysis of Leviticus 18 shows the incest prohibitions to be a coherent later priestly system defining forbidden degrees of kinship, and Calum Carmichael argues, more speculatively, that these laws were partly framed with the patriarchal narratives in view — the lawgiver legislating against precisely the unions the ancestors had contracted. On this reading the texts do not so much flatly contradict as document a development: older narrative preserving earlier norms, later codes systematizing prohibitions that the ancestors' own conduct would have violated.

It is worth distinguishing the half-sister case from the aunt prohibitions also cited in the cluster (Lev 18:12; 20:19 forbid the father's or mother's sister). Those concern a different degree of kinship and are not what Abraham's relationship to Sarah involves; the relevant verses for the contradiction are Leviticus 18:9, 20:17, and Deuteronomy 27:22, all of which name the paternal half-sister explicitly. Verdict: partially harmonized — the chronological defense legitimately removes the charge that Abraham broke an existing law, but it concedes the moral-substantive tension and cannot be paired with the failed 'loose sister' reading, which Genesis 20:12's own precision refutes.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The chronological harmonization is valid in principle: the Levitical and Deuteronomic incest codes are presented as Sinai-era legislation post-dating Abraham, so the patriarch is not narrated as violating a law not yet given. That dissolves the formal legal contradiction, but it concedes the substantive moral tension and cannot be combined with the alternative 'sister means something looser' defense, which the precise wording of Gen 20:12 refutes.

commentary_out.change_summary: Per audit, softened the Lev 20:17 chesed gloss to note the 'disgrace/shame' sense and the debated (possibly homonymous) relationship to covenant-loyalty chesed rather than asserting it is the loyalty word used pejoratively.

issues.problem: The philological note on Lev 20:17 reads the Hebrew term for 'wicked thing' as 'chesed.' The Masoretic term in Lev 20:17 is indeed chesed (חֶסֶד) used in the pejorative 'disgrace/shame' sense, and the commentary's cautious framing (possible homonym from a separate root vs. the covenant-loyalty word) is responsible and accurate. This is correctly handled. However, the transliteration 'chesed' for both the disgrace term and loyalty term may mislead some readers since they are sometimes distinguished in vocalization; the caution is adequate but could note the standard distinction more precisely.
issues.correction: Optionally note that the disgrace term and the loyalty term, though both transliterated chesed, are widely treated by lexicographers as homonyms (HALOT lists distinct entries). The existing caution is substantially adequate.

issues.problem: The Greengus citation ('Sisterhood Adoption at Nuzi and the "Wife-Sister" in Genesis,' HUCA 46 [1975], 5-31) and the attribution that Greengus refuted Speiser's Nuzi wife-sister thesis are accurate and a strong, fair handling. Speiser's thesis and its rejection are correctly represented. The treatment of the two harmonizations as mutually undermining is a fair, non-strawmanned analysis.

entries.question: Is it OK to swear?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 6:13, Isaiah 65:16, and Jeremiah 4:2 and 12:16 all positively command swearing by Yahweh's name. Matthew 5:34-37 has Jesus saying "swear not at all" — no heaven, no earth, just yes-yes and no-no, and anything more "cometh of evil." Torah makes oaths by God's name an act of covenantal loyalty; Jesus makes them a moral problem.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic — D. A. Carson runs this in his Matthew commentary, and Craig Blomberg takes the same line — is that Jesus isn't abolishing oaths per se, he's forbidding the casuistic abuse of oaths that first-century Jewish legal culture had developed, where you could swear by "Jerusalem" or "your head" to sound binding without actually being legally bound. Matthew 23:16-22 supports this reading: Jesus condemns the "you swear by the temple, it's nothing, but swear by the gold of the temple, you're bound" system. Fair. But the Sermon on the Mount formula is categorical — "swear not at all" — and the Epistle of James 5:12 repeats it just as categorically. Early Christian groups (the Anabaptists, the Quakers) read this as a straight prohibition for centuries, and they weren't wrong about the plain sense. Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in their ICC Matthew argue Jesus is radicalizing Torah here in the same pattern as the other antitheses in Matthew 5 — taking a Torah allowance (oaths by the Name) and canceling it under the inbreaking kingdom. That's a genuine contradiction with Deuteronomy 6:13, not a casuistic footnote. The harmonization works if you allow Jesus to be selectively overriding Torah; it just doesn't work if you need the Old Testament and Jesus to be saying the same thing.
entries.scholarship: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, *The Gospel According to Saint Matthew* (International Critical Commentary; T&T Clark, 1988), on Matt 5:33-37. D. A. Carson, *Matthew* (Expositor's Bible Commentary; Zondervan, 1984). Craig L. Blomberg, *Matthew* (New American Commentary 22; B&H, 1992). Ulrich Luz, *Matthew 1-7: A Commentary* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 2007).

commentary_out.commentary:
The Hebrew Bible does not merely tolerate oaths in Yahweh's name; it commands them as acts of covenant fidelity. Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20 pair fearing God, serving him, and swearing by his name as a single triad of loyalty, deliberately contrasting Israelite oaths with oaths sworn by foreign gods. Isaiah 65:16 envisions a future in which people swear "by the God of truth" (*bēʾlōhê ʾāmēn*), and Jeremiah 4:2 and 12:16 make swearing "the LORD lives" (*ḥay-YHWH*) the mark of a converted, restored nation. To swear by Yahweh's name was to confess his exclusive lordship; in this stream of thought, refusing to swear by it could itself verge on apostasy, since the practical alternative was swearing by other gods.

Matthew 5:34-37 cuts against this. The Greek is emphatic: *egō de legō hymin mē omosai holōs* — "but I say to you, do not swear at all." *Holōs* ("at all," "wholly") is categorical, and the four prohibited oath-formulas (by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, by one's head) are followed by the demand that speech be simply "yes yes, no no," with anything beyond this *ek tou ponērou* — "from the evil one" or "of evil." James 5:12, almost certainly drawing on the same dominical tradition, repeats the prohibition with equal force: "above all, my brothers, do not swear" (*Pro pantōn de, adelphoi mou, mē omnyete*).

The standard harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg, is that Jesus targets not oaths as such but the casuistic abuse of oaths in first-century Judaism, whereby swearing by lesser things (Jerusalem, one's head, the gold of the temple) created an escape hatch from binding obligation. Matthew 23:16-22 lends this real support: there Jesus explicitly attacks the graded system in which swearing by the temple counts for nothing but swearing by its gold binds. On this reading, Jesus demands a transparent truthfulness that makes oaths superfluous, not the abolition of the lawful Yahwistic oath. The argument is serious and is partially correct about the abuses being addressed.

It nonetheless strains against the categorical form of the saying and against the reception history. The Essenes, per Josephus (*Jewish War* 2.135), avoided oaths altogether and held that one who is not believed without invoking God stands already condemned; Sirach 23:9-11 warns against habituating the mouth to oaths. Jesus' formula stands in this stream of intensified piety and reads most naturally as an absolute. Significant strands of the early church took it so: Justin Martyr cites "swear not at all" as a binding command of Christ (1 Apology 16), and the Anabaptists and later the Quakers refused all oaths on the strength of these verses — and they were not misreading the plain sense. (The Didache, by contrast, should not be enlisted here: Did. 2.3 forbids false and perjured oaths, echoing the Decalogue, not all swearing.) Davies and Allison, in the ICC, locate the saying within the structure of Matthew's antitheses ("you have heard... but I say to you"), where Jesus characteristically intensifies or transcends a Torah provision — here a provision that not only permitted but commanded oaths. Ulrich Luz in Hermeneia likewise reads it as a radicalization rather than a mere clarification of abuse.

The distinction matters because the harmonization succeeds only by narrowing "swear not at all" to "swear not abusively." If one grants that Jesus is sharpening and partly overriding Torah under the inbreaking kingdom — the same move he makes on divorce (Matt 5:31-32) and retaliation (5:38-39), neither of which is a mere policing of misuse — then the relationship to Deuteronomy 6:13 is one of deliberate transcendence: not contradiction in the sense of a logical blunder by a single author, but genuine tension between two normative positions advanced by two traditions. What cannot be sustained is the claim that Deuteronomy's command to swear and Jesus' command not to swear say the same thing. Deuteronomy makes the oath a positive act of fidelity; Matthew makes it, at minimum, a concession to a fallen condition and, on its face, something to be renounced. Verdict: genuine tension, harmonizable only by conceding that Jesus revises the Torah's positive command rather than merely correcting its abuse.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The casuistic-abuse reading (supported by Matt 23:16-22 and Sirach 23) accounts for the oath-formulas Jesus targets, and the tension reduces if one allows that Jesus, in the antithesis form, intensifies and partly overrides the Torah's positive command rather than addressing the same question identically; it does not dissolve the substantive difference from Deut 6:13.

entries.question: Has God ever tempted anyone?
entries.summary: James 1:13 draws a hard line: "God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man." Genesis 22:1 opens the Akedah by saying "God did tempt Abraham" and tells him to sacrifice Isaac. The KJV translates the same Hebrew and Greek roots consistently, which is why this reads as a contradiction in English.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer, Wenham, and Douglas Moo in his James commentary resolve this through translation: the Hebrew verb *nissah* in Genesis 22:1 means "test" or "prove," not "tempt" in the James 1:13 sense of luring toward evil. Modern translations (NIV, NRSV, ESV) render Genesis 22:1 as "tested" precisely to dodge the semantic collision. That's a legitimate philological point — *nissah* and the Greek *peirazō* in James 1:13 overlap but aren't identical, and James is clearly talking about enticement toward sin, while Genesis 22 is a loyalty test. So in modern translation the contradiction softens. BUT — and this is the critical wrinkle — the KJV reading isn't wrong, it's just old. The underlying theological problem doesn't go away: whether you call it "testing" or "tempting," God is in Genesis 22 deliberately commanding Abraham to commit what Torah elsewhere defines as abomination (human sacrifice, Lev 18:21, Deut 12:31). James 1:13 says God "cannot be tempted with evil" — but Genesis 22 has God commanding evil as a loyalty check. Jon Levenson's *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* digs into how uncomfortable this made ancient interpreters, who went to enormous lengths (LXX renderings, Jubilees 17-18 blaming Mastema/Satan for the prompt) to get God out of directly initiating the test. The translation fix saves the verses; it doesn't save the theological problem.
entries.scholarship: Douglas J. Moo, *The Letter of James* (Pillar New Testament Commentary; Eerdmans, 2000). Gordon J. Wenham, *Genesis 16-50* (Word Biblical Commentary 2; Word, 1994), on Gen 22:1. Jon D. Levenson, *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* (Yale University Press, 1993). James L. Kugel, *Traditions of the Bible* (Harvard University Press, 1998). Gleason L. Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

commentary_out.commentary:
James 1:13 makes a doubled claim about God and temptation: God is *apeirastos kakōn* and he himself "tempts no one" (*peirazei de autos oudena*). The governing verb is *peirazō*. Genesis 22:1 in the Septuagint uses the same root: *ho theos epeirazen ton Abraam*, "God tested Abraham," rendering the Hebrew *wĕhāʾĕlōhîm nissāh ʾet-ʾabrāhām*. Because the King James Version translates both *nissah* and *peirazō* with "tempt," the English reader meets a flat contradiction: God tempted Abraham (Gen 22:1) versus God tempts no one (James 1:13).

A caveat must be entered before the harmonization is weighed, because the harmonization leans on it. *Apeirastos* is a New Testament hapax legomenon, and its sense is genuinely contested. The phrase *apeirastos kakōn* admits at least two readings: a passive construal, "God cannot be tempted by evil things," and an alternative sometimes defended on the strength of the adjective's verbal form and the genitive, roughly "God is inexperienced in evil" or "ought not to be tested in matters of evil" (compare the cognate complaint that the wilderness generation "tested" God). The standard lexica and most commentators favor the passive sense, but the point is not settled, and the harmonization that follows assumes precisely that passive reading. If one adopted the "should not be tested" sense, the verse would be making a different claim and the comparison with Genesis 22 would shift accordingly. Honest treatment flags that the adopted rendering is the contested one.

Granting the passive sense, the most respectable harmonization is lexical and contextual, and it is largely sound. Hebrew *nissah* denotes proving, testing, or trying — God tests Israel in the wilderness (Exod 16:4; Deut 8:2, 16) to know and refine what is in their heart — and carries no necessary sense of enticement toward evil. James 1:13-15, by contrast, defines the *peirasmos* in view precisely as the inward pull of *epithymia* ("desire") that, once conceived, "gives birth to sin," and sin "to death." James excludes God as the *source of moral enticement*; Genesis 22 presents God administering a loyalty trial. The two texts use overlapping vocabulary for distinguishable acts. Douglas Moo and Gordon Wenham both make this point, and modern versions (NIV, NRSV, ESV) render Genesis 22:1 "tested" exactly to forestall the collision. At the level of word-sense the English contradiction is an artifact of seventeenth-century usage, in which "tempt" still meant simply "to test."

What the lexical solution does not touch is the residual theological problem. Even granting "test" rather than "entice," Genesis 22 has God commanding Abraham to perform an act the same canon brands an abomination — the slaughter of his son as a burnt offering (cf. Lev 18:21; Deut 12:31, which condemn child sacrifice as the detestable practice of the nations). James asserts that God stands wholly apart from evil; Genesis 22 has God initiate a trial whose stipulated content is the killing of a child. The discomfort this produced in antiquity is itself a historical datum. Jon Levenson documents how the Akedah was theologically domesticated across centuries of Jewish and Christian reading, and the Book of Jubilees (17:15-18:13) rewrites the scene so that Prince Mastema, the chief of hostility, proposes the test (17:15-16), with the binding narrated through chapter 18 — exactly the maneuver James 1:13 performs in shifting the origin of temptation away from God onto an external or inner agent. The Genesis narrator, by contrast, attributes the prompt directly and unflinchingly to God (22:1-2). James Kugel surveys the ancient interpretive contortions provoked by the wish to keep God's hands clean of initiating so dark a command.

The strongest apologetic synthesis distinguishes two categories: God may *test* fidelity (Gen 22) without *tempting* toward sin (James 1:13), since a test aims at proving and strengthening faith while a temptation aims at producing sin. This is coherent, and most critical scholars would grant it for the words *as such*; the verbal contradiction genuinely dissolves. Where it falters is on the moral content of this particular test. A test whose obedient outcome would be the ritual killing of a child is not obviously distinguishable from solicitation to evil, and James' own framework sits uneasily beside a divine command whose face value is to kill an innocent. The provision of the ram (22:13) resolves the narrative but not the categorical claim. That the angel, not God directly, halts the act, and that later tradition reassigns the prompt to Mastema, shows interpreters working precisely at this seam.

Verdict: the verbal contradiction is a translation artifact that dissolves on the *nissah*/*peirazō* distinction (assuming the passive sense of the contested *apeirastos kakōn*); the underlying theological tension between James 1:13 and the moral content of the Akedah is real and was felt acutely by ancient interpreters.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The verbal clash is a KJV translation artifact: Hebrew nissah and the relevant sense of peirazō denote 'test/prove,' whereas James 1:13 expressly defines temptation as enticement toward sin via inner desire, so the two texts use overlapping vocabulary for distinguishable acts; the residual theological tension over the moral content of the Akedah is not thereby resolved. The harmonization also presupposes the passive construal of the contested phrase apeirastos kakōn.
